opus-5.5.text:
I think what I really hope is that AMI Labs can be a kind of existence proof. For a lot of young researchers right now, especially PhD students or junior faculty, there's this feeling that the only path that matters is the one everyone is already on: scale up language models, chase the benchmarks, join a big lab, and become one small piece of a very large machine. That path is valuable, I'm not dismissing it. But it creates a monoculture, and monocultures are fragile, both scientifically and for the people inside them.

What we're trying to do is take a bet on a different set of ideas: world models, learning from sensory data, systems that can understand and predict the physical world, plan, and reason, rather than just predict the next token. Whether or not every specific idea works out, I want young people to see that you can take a contrarian scientific position seriously, put real resources behind it, and do it in a way that stays open and rigorous.

The second thing is culture. I spent a lot of time in academia, and I really value its spirit: curiosity, publishing, sharing code, letting students own their ideas. I don't want AMI to feel like you have to give that up the moment you leave a university. I hope it can be a place where people with an academic soul can do research at a scale that's hard to get in a university lab, without becoming purely product-driven.

And finally, I hope it gives people a bit of courage. A lot of the most important ideas in this field, including deep learning itself, were unfashionable for a long time. If a young person has a strange idea they really believe in, I want them to know there are places, and people, who will take it seriously. Not because it's guaranteed to work, but because the field needs people who are willing to be wrong in interesting ways.

r001.rationale: The response says young researchers face a dominant path and presents AMI as putting real resources behind a different set of ideas, addressing the lack of support for unconventional work.

r002.rationale: It describes AMI as a place for researchers to do research, but does not say young academics can participate without becoming company employees.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, actually, because I came out of academia myself and I know what it feels like when you have an idea that doesn't fit the mold.

Right now, if you're a PhD student or a young faculty member, the incentives push you toward a very narrow path. You need papers, you need citations, you need to work on whatever the dominant paradigm is because that's what gets accepted. If you want to step outside of that, to say "I don't think scaling the current recipe is the whole answer, I want to try something structurally different," it's very hard. You often don't have the compute, you don't have the engineering support, and honestly you don't have the permission. There's a real cost to being wrong when you're early in your career.

So what I hope AMI can do is be a place where that kind of bet is not just tolerated but actively encouraged. We're explicitly interested in questions that the mainstream has sort of set aside: world models, how systems build representations of the physical world, learning from observation rather than just from text, planning and reasoning that isn't purely autoregressive. These are long-horizon problems. They don't pay off in a six-month paper cycle.

I don't want to oversell it. We're not a university and we won't replace what universities do. But I think there are a few concrete things we can offer. One is resources: giving a young researcher the ability to actually test a non-mainstream idea at a meaningful scale, instead of running toy experiments and getting told it doesn't work. Another is community. If you're the only person in your department who thinks the current approach has fundamental limits, that's very lonely. Having a group of people who share that intuition and can argue with you seriously about it matters a lot. And the third is just time. Protecting people from the pressure to publish incrementally so they can think about the harder question.

What I tell students is this: the field moves so fast that the safest-looking path, following the leaderboard, is actually not that safe, because by the time you catch up, the frontier has moved. The really valuable thing is to develop your own taste, your own view of what's missing. And I'd like AMI to be a place where someone with that taste, even if they're unproven, can come and actually try it.

r001.rationale: It says young researchers often lack compute and engineering support to test ideas outside the dominant paradigm, and hopes AMI can provide resources to test them at meaningful scale.

r002.rationale: AMI is described as a place where young researchers can come and try unconventional ideas, but the response does not say they can participate without becoming company employees.

astra-6.text:
I hope AMI Labs can give them another path—a place where they can pursue ambitious research without feeling that there’s only one way to build a career. For a young researcher, it can be difficult to work on something that doesn’t fit neatly into what everyone else is doing. You need time, support, and people who are willing to take the question seriously before there’s a clear result.

That’s the kind of environment I hope we can help create. It shouldn’t be about telling young people to leave academia. It should be about giving them more options, and making it possible to follow an idea they really believe in, even when the outcome is uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response says unconventional work can be hard to pursue and calls for another path with time, support, and people willing to take the question seriously.

r002.rationale: It says AMI Labs should give young people more options without urging them to leave academia, but does not say they can participate in AMI Labs’ work without becoming employees.

sol-6.1.text:
I hope AMI Labs can show young researchers that there are different ways to do meaningful research. If you’re in academia and you have an idea that doesn’t fit the mainstream, it can be hard to find the space and support to pursue it. Ideally, we can help create that space—somewhere people can ask fundamental questions, try things that might fail, and work toward something they really believe in.

And that doesn’t necessarily mean everyone should leave academia or join a company. I’d like young people to feel that they have more choices, and that doing something different is a legitimate choice.

r001.rationale: It says ideas outside the mainstream can be hard to find the space and support to pursue, identifying a lack of support and opportunity as a constraint.

r002.rationale: It says young people need not join a company, but does not propose that they can participate in AMI Labs’ work without becoming employees.
